messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kiet is a 40-year-old divorced journalist of Vietnamese heritage who was kidnapped and tortured while investigating forced labour camps in a neighbouring country. For three weeks he was blindfolded, beaten, starved, and forced to listen as other prisoners—children among them—cried in adjacent cells. He was eventually released in a prisoner exchange, but the physical and psychological scars remained deeply embedded.

In the months that followed, Kiet found himself unable to return to his previous life. He began to notice that the sound of a child crying—any child, anywhere—would send a jolt of electricity through his chest, and in those moments his memory of the cell would feel vivid yet impossible, as though the whole ordeal had happened to someone else. Hearing a name that resembled one of his captors would trigger a visceral sense of dizziness, leaving him lightheaded and convinced that others could see the shame written on his face. That feeling that people could read his history just by looking at him made him certain he was fundamentally broken, and he started avoiding colleagues he had socialised with before the kidnapping, certain they pitied or judged him.

What frightened Kiet most was how ordinary sounds now made him jump. A car door slamming, a spoon clattering against a bowl—each unexpected noise reignited the hypervigilance he had relied on in captivity. When he found himself scanning faces in a coffee shop for signs of threat, he would be flooded with guilt and anger, believing that his cooperation under torture—giving up a source’s name—had violated his core ethics. He dwelled endlessly on how he could have prevented his capture, replaying decisions with a tight, obsessive focus, which only amplified his startle response and made him more vigilant. He also stopped eating properly, restricting food as a way to regain control; but the resulting light-headedness often made him feel dizzy again, and that dizziness would pull him back into the unreal fragments of his memory.

Kiet’s memory of the torture itself was riddled with gaps. Deliberate effort to recall only brought up disjointed sensations—pressure on his wrists, the taste of blood—but never a coherent story. The gaps themselves felt threatening, as if something hidden might ambush him, and they reinforced his belief that he was defective, that his mind had broken. In turn, his hypervigilance made deliberate recall even harder, because he was always scanning, never able to sit still with the past. When he did catch a glimpse of a memory, it felt so extreme that he found it hard to accept it had really happened; that sense of unreality only deepened his conviction that others saw him as damaged.

As weeks turned into months, Kiet’s avoidance narrowed his world. He stopped going to the newsroom, worked from home, and saw almost no one. His ex-wife had stopped calling after he cancelled their son’s visit three times—the boy’s crying had become unbearable. The loneliness fed his rumination, and rumination brought him back to the memory gaps, which in turn drove him to restrict food even more. He came to believe that the more he ate, the more he would feel his body and the more his past would surface. The cycle was tightening, and he could feel his career slipping away.

What finally brought Kiet to seek help was a breakdown during a routine assignment: a colleague mentioned a name similar to his torturer’s, and Kiet became so dizzy and nauseated that he had to be taken to the emergency room. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, but also quietly desperate to believe that the person he was before—a reporter who trusted his own instincts—still exists somewhere beneath the shame and the startle.

violation_explanations: No paragraph conveys that negative appraisals (e.g., beliefs of being broken or judged) cause or heighten sensitivity to triggers.
No paragraph conveys that memory (gaps, fragments) leads to the experience or detection of triggers.
No paragraph conveys that threat (hypervigilance, startle) directly causes the occurrence or salience of triggers.
No paragraph conveys that maladaptive strategies (avoidance, food restriction) lead to the emergence or perception of triggers.
